t: 3738. Longest Non-Decreasing Subarray After Replacing at Most One Element
o: Precompute pre[i] = length of the longest non-decreasing run ending at i, and suf[i] = length of the run starting at i. Every descent (nums[i] > nums[i+1]) is the only place a replacement helps. Replacing nums[i] extends the left run and, when nums[i-1] ≤ nums[i+1], also bridges into the right run; symmetrically for replacing nums[i+1]. The answer is the max over all such candidates and the untouched best run. Example [1,2,3,1,2]: descent at (3,1); replacing the 1 with 3 gives run length pre[2]+1 = 4.
k: Only positions adjacent to a descent matter; elsewhere the array is already locally non-decreasing.
A replacement bridges two runs iff the neighbors allow a common value, i.e., nums[left neighbor] ≤ nums[right neighbor].

a.n: Approach 1: pre/suf Arrays + Descent Case Analysis
a.i: As described: DP arrays for run lengths, then examine each descent with two replacement choices.
s: Fill pre left-to-right and suf right-to-left.

For each i with nums[i] > nums[i+1]: candidate replacing nums[i] = (pre[i-1] if i>0 else 0) + 1 + (suf[i+1] if i>0 and nums[i-1] <= nums[i+1] else suf[i+1] if i==0 else 0); candidate replacing nums[i+1] analogously with suf[i+2]/pre[i] and condition nums[i] <= nums[i+2].
a.sp: O(n) for the two DP arrays

w: Test edge cases: single element (answer 1), strictly decreasing arrays (answer 2), and arrays where the best fix is at either boundary. Common bug: assuming a replacement always merges both sides — the bridge condition nums[a] ≤ nums[b] is essential. Follow-up: allow k replacements (DP with state = replacements used).
